questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Technology found outside the roadmap
questions.question: A risk practitioner at an insurance broker learns the marketing team has used an unapproved cloud survey tool for six months to collect client contact details. What should the practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Find the tool's business owner and assess its risk against appetite
options.B: Have IT block the tool until the business owner reviews its security
options.C: Approve the tool on the roadmap and assess it at year end
options.D: Report the marketing team's policy breach to the compliance function

questions.key_concept: Technology adopted outside the roadmap is assessed with its business owner against appetite before anyone blocks or approves it.
questions.pre_read: Notice how long the tool has been in use and what data it holds, then weigh the timing of each option.
questions.correct_explanation: An unapproved tool is a risk to understand before it is a problem to remove. Finding the business owner gives the risk an accountable decision-maker, and assessing it against appetite shows whether the client data exposure needs urgent treatment. Blocking first acts before analysis: it may disrupt a working process, push staff to another workaround and still leave six months of collected data unassessed.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice, because it stops new exposure. But blocking before analysis can disrupt the business and leaves the data already collected unassessed; containment follows a risk-based decision.
wrong_explanations.C: Approving now and assessing later reverses the order: the client data risk would stay unexamined for months.
wrong_explanations.D: A policy breach may need reporting later, but treating it as a conduct matter first leaves the client data risk unanalyzed and unowned.

tips: Eliminate: C approves the tool before any risk review, and D treats a data risk as a conduct issue before anyone knows its size.
Final two: A beats B because the practitioner finds an owner and analyzes before acting; blocking first is a response chosen without knowing the risk.
Exam cue: for shadow IT found in use, the FIRST step is usually to identify the owner and assess the risk, not to ban or approve the tool.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.AM-02 (inventories of software, services and systems managed by the organization are maintained); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A1.2 Technology Roadmaps and Off-Roadmap Technology (assess off-roadmap technology with its owner instead of banning or approving it). Original insurance broker survey-tool scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D4 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): lens words added to distractors B and C; pre_read made non-revealing; C rewritten without a reason tail. Cross-domain fix 30 Oct 2026: 'business' added to distractor B so the lens word is not key-only.

questions.subtopic: 4A1 Technology roadmaps and enterprise architecture (EA). Legacy system risk
questions.question: At a county court service, the operations manager says a case-filing system on unsupported software needs no risk entry because it has not failed in twelve years. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Rate the likelihood as low against appetite from its clean record
options.B: Log the risk with an owner and rate it against appetite
options.C: Ask internal audit to test the system before recording any risk
options.D: Run a vulnerability scan to assess exposure before recording risk

questions.key_concept: Legacy and unsupported systems belong in the risk register with a business owner, whatever their reliability record.
questions.pre_read: Separate the manager's evidence from the facts in the stem that drive the risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Unsupported software is a known exposure whatever its track record: no patches arrive, skills fade and the impact stays tied to court filings. Logging the risk with an accountable owner makes someone accountable, and rating it against appetite shows whether action is needed. A scan adds useful evidence for the rating, but waiting for it before recording leaves a known risk invisible and unowned.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the system has been reliable. But past uptime says nothing about missing patches; the likelihood of compromise rises once support ends, and the impact is unchanged.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit gives independent assurance; it does not run the risk register. Recording and rating the risk is the practitioner's job and should not wait for an audit.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: scan results sharpen the rating. But unsupported software is already a known risk, so it is recorded and owned now, with the scan informing the analysis.

tips: Eliminate: A reads past reliability as low likelihood, and C hands the practitioner's risk recording to internal audit, which gives assurance but does not run the register.
Final two: B beats D because a known exposure is recorded and owned first; scans refine the rating but are not a gate before the risk becomes visible.
Exam cue: 'it still works' is never a risk assessment. Legacy and unsupported systems go in the register with a business owner, then get rated.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-22 (Unsupported System Components); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.PS-02 (software is maintained, replaced and removed commensurate with risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A1.3 Technical Debt and Legacy Systems (exam trap: leaving a reliable legacy system off the register). Original county court case-filing scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D4 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): C names a business owner (audit); A loses its 'since' tail and carries 'appetite'; D carries 'assess' (blind de-cue); tip 3 quotes the phrase; pre_read non-revealing; options re-lettered (key now B) to break the key cycle; option lengths evened. Cross-domain fix 30 Oct 2026: key B reworded to 'an owner' so 'business' is not key-only.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. Change process findings
questions.question: A risk practitioner reviews a retailer's change management process after two outages. Which finding should concern the practitioner MOST?

options.A: Standard changes go live with no change advisory board review
options.B: Team leads act as change authority for low-risk normal changes
options.C: The change advisory board meets weekly rather than before each change
options.D: Emergency changes bypass the board and are seldom reviewed afterward

questions.key_concept: Emergency changes are acceptable only when each one receives a timely after-the-fact review.
questions.pre_read: Sort the findings into design choices and real control gaps before judging which matters most.
questions.correct_explanation: Emergency changes may bypass the normal approval path only because a review follows soon after. When few are reviewed afterward, untested or unauthorized changes sit in production unseen, a plausible cause of the outages. Standard changes without board review are working as designed: they are pre-approved, low-risk and run from a set procedure, so the missing check there is intended, not a gap.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice, since it also sounds like missing review. But standard changes are pre-approved by design because they are low risk and repeatable.
wrong_explanations.B: Delegating change authority for low-risk changes to team leads matches review effort to risk, which is sound design rather than a gap.
wrong_explanations.C: A weekly board is normal practice; urgent work goes through the emergency route. Meeting cadence is not a weakness in itself.

tips: Eliminate: C describes a normal board cadence, and B describes risk-based delegation of approval; both are design choices, not weaknesses.
Final two: D beats A because standard changes are pre-approved by design, while emergency changes depend on an after-the-fact review that is not happening.
Exam cue: when a control lets a step be skipped, look for the follow-up check that makes skipping safe; a missing follow-up is the real gap.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-128 Section 3.3.2 (Implement the Configuration Change Control Process: unscheduled changes are reviewed by the CCB as soon as practical); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A2.1 Change and Configuration Management (emergency changes need a timely retrospective review; standard changes are pre-approved). Original retailer outage scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D4 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): B no longer overstates emergency practice; D uses 'change authority'; explanation matches 'seldom'; options re-lettered (key now D) to break the key cycle; C length evened.

questions.subtopic: 4A2 Operations management. Recurring service failures
questions.question: Self-service check-in kiosks at a regional airline freeze several times a month, and the service desk restores each one within minutes and closes the ticket. What should the risk practitioner recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Set a tighter target for restoring each kiosk within five minutes
options.B: Replace the kiosks with a newer model from a different vendor
options.C: Track kiosk outages as a key risk indicator on the dashboard
options.D: Raise a problem record to find and permanently remove the root cause

questions.key_concept: Incident management restores service; problem management removes the root cause of repeated incidents.
questions.pre_read: Notice how often the same failure returns and what each option would change about it.
questions.correct_explanation: Repeated incidents with the same symptom point to an unresolved cause. Incident management has done its job by restoring service; problem management now needs to find why the kiosks freeze and remove the cause through a controlled change, which lowers future likelihood. Tracking outages as an indicator is useful monitoring, but it only measures the risk; it does not reduce it.

wrong_explanations.A: A tighter restore target improves incident handling but leaves the cause in place, so the freezes and passenger delays keep recurring.
wrong_explanations.B: Replacing hardware before the cause is known may not fix it; the fault could be software, network or configuration, and the money may be wasted.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: an indicator makes the trend visible to owners. But measuring recurrence does not stop it; the root cause still needs to be found.

tips: Eliminate: A speeds up incident handling without touching the cause, and B picks a fix before root cause analysis shows what is actually failing.
Final two: D beats C because problem management removes the cause and lowers likelihood, while an indicator only reports a risk that keeps recurring.
Exam cue: repeated incidents with the same symptom call for problem management and root cause analysis, not faster restores.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 RS.AN-03 (analysis is performed to establish what has taken place during an incident and the root cause of the incident); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.IM-03 (improvements are identified from execution of operational processes, procedures and activities)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A2.2 Incident and Problem Management (fast closure is not risk reduction; repeats call for a problem record). Original airline kiosk scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D4 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): pre_read made non-revealing.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). Acceptance testing roles
questions.question: To meet a launch date, a university's project manager plans to have developers run user acceptance testing on a new student-fees system. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Allow it if developers document every test case and its result
options.B: Ask internal audit to review the test results before go-live
options.C: Have finance users perform and sign off the acceptance testing
options.D: Delay launch until an external testing firm completes the tests

questions.key_concept: User acceptance testing is performed and signed off by business users, independent of the developers who built the system.
questions.pre_read: Ask what acceptance testing is meant to prove, and who is able to prove it.
questions.correct_explanation: User acceptance testing confirms that the system meets the business's needs, so the people who will rely on it, here finance staff, should run it and sign it off. That keeps the check independent of the builders and puts acceptance with the business. An external firm adds independence but cannot judge business fit, and delaying the launch is the sponsor's decision, not the practitioner's.

wrong_explanations.A: Documentation records what developers tested, but they still test against their own understanding, so the check is neither independent nor business-led.
wrong_explanations.B: Internal audit provides assurance on the process, not acceptance of the system. Reviewing results after the fact does not replace testing by users.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: an external firm is independent of the developers. But only users can confirm business fit, and launch dates belong to the sponsor.

tips: Eliminate: A documents developer testing without making it independent, and B gives the job to internal audit, whose role is assurance, not system acceptance.
Final two: C beats D because acceptance is about business needs, so business users test and sign off; outside testers are independent but cannot judge fit.
Exam cue: in SDLC items, developers build and test their code, business users accept the system, and owners accept residual risk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-3 (System Development Life Cycle); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A3.1 Risk Across the SDLC Phases (exam trap: developers performing user acceptance testing). Original university student-fees scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D4 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026.

questions.subtopic: 4A3 System development life cycle (SDLC). Third-party AI model update
questions.question: A health insurer's chatbot vendor will replace the underlying AI model next month, saying the interface and prices stay the same. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Watch customer complaints after the swap and escalate any rise
options.B: Rely on the vendor's assurance that the service will work as before
options.C: Handle the swap as a change, validating the new model before use
options.D: Ask the vendor to keep the current model under the existing contract

questions.key_concept: A vendor's change to the AI model behind a service is a change that needs validation before use.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the vendor says will stay the same, and what it does not mention.
questions.correct_explanation: A new model can answer the same questions differently even when the interface and price stay fixed, so the swap is a change to a member-facing process. Treating it as one means the insurer's owner sees validation results, such as accuracy and harmful-answer tests, before members are exposed. Monitoring complaints is a useful second layer, but it detects harm only after members have received wrong answers.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: monitoring catches problems in production. But it is detective and late; members would already have received any wrong or harmful answers.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the vendor knows its own service. But behavior lives in the model, not the interface, and the insurer stays accountable for the answers its members receive.
wrong_explanations.D: Freezing the vendor's model resists normal change instead of managing it, and the vendor may refuse; assessing the new model is the risk-based step.

tips: Eliminate: B trusts the vendor's word that behavior will not change, and D tries to stop the vendor's change instead of assessing it.
Final two: C beats A because validating before use prevents harm to members, while complaint monitoring only detects it after the new model is live.
Exam cue: a new model, new training data or a retrained model is a change, even from a vendor; validate and approve it before go-live.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 3.1 (AI risks and benefits from third-party resources are regularly monitored and risk controls are applied and documented); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-4 (Impact Analyses)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A3.3 AI Models in the SDLC (a model change is a change; validate and approve before deployment), applied to a vendor-hosted model. Original health insurer chatbot scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D4 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. AI item. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): B loses its 'since' tail; tip 1 and why-B updated; pre_read non-revealing; options re-lettered (key now C) to break the key cycle.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Approving a new data use
questions.question: A grocery chain's analytics team wants to copy loyalty-card purchase records into a new reporting tool. Who should the risk practitioner advise is the MOST appropriate person to approve this new use?

options.A: The business manager accountable for the customer records
options.B: The risk analyst who assessed the reporting tool's security
options.C: The CISO, who sets the organization's data security policy
options.D: The IT manager who runs the database for the business

questions.key_concept: The data owner, an accountable business manager, approves access to and new uses of data; IT is the custodian.
questions.pre_read: For each person named, ask what their role lets them decide about the data.
questions.correct_explanation: The data owner, the business manager accountable for the customer records, sets the rules for using the data. They can judge whether the reporting use fits the purpose the data was collected for and its classification. The CISO sets security policy and advises on controls, but does not own business data or decide its uses; the IT manager is the custodian who carries out the owner's rules.

wrong_explanations.B: The analyst assesses and advises on the tool's risk; approving a new use of business data is the data owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the CISO sets security policy and can advise on controls. But policy authority is not data ownership; the accountable business manager approves uses.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because IT runs the database. But IT is the custodian: it applies the owner's rules and cannot judge the data's business value or permitted uses.

tips: Eliminate: D names the custodian, who carries out the owner's rules, and B names the risk analyst, who advises but does not approve uses of business data.
Final two: A beats C because data ownership sits with the accountable business manager; the CISO sets security policy but does not decide business uses.
Exam cue: who decides access, use or retention of data? The data owner, a business role, not IT, security or the risk function.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Information Owner/Steward)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A4.1 Data Lifecycle, Classification and Ownership (data belongs to the business; IT is custodian). Original grocery loyalty-data scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D4 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): stem names the risk practitioner (rule 8); pre_read made non-revealing; options re-lettered (key now A) to break the key cycle. Cross-domain fix 30 Oct 2026: 'business' added to distractor D so the lens word is not key-only.

questions.subtopic: 4A4 Data lifecycle management. Sanitizing solid-state media
questions.question: A school district will donate retired staff laptops whose solid-state drives held student records. Which approach should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST for making the data unrecoverable?

options.A: Delete the user folders and empty the recycle bin on each laptop
options.B: Purge each drive with a method such as cryptographic erase
options.C: Reformat each drive and reinstall a clean operating system
options.D: Overwrite each drive with zeros once using standard disk software

questions.key_concept: Sanitization must match the media: solid-state drives need a purge method, and the result is recorded.
questions.pre_read: Note the drive type and that the laptops must stay usable, then rule out methods that leave data behind.
questions.correct_explanation: Solid-state drives spread data across spare cells that normal writes cannot reach, so deleting, reformatting or a standard overwrite can leave student records recoverable. A purge method such as cryptographic erase defeats laboratory recovery while keeping the laptops usable for donation. Recording the method and result gives evidence the data owner can rely on. Overwriting is a valid clear method on magnetic disks, not a reliable one here.

wrong_explanations.A: Deleting files removes pointers, not data; common recovery tools can often restore deleted student records.
wrong_explanations.C: Reformatting rebuilds the file system but usually leaves the underlying data in place and recoverable.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: overwriting is a recognized clear method on magnetic disks. On solid-state drives, wear leveling leaves cells the overwrite never reaches.

tips: Eliminate: A and C only remove file pointers or the file system, so the records stay recoverable with common tools.
Final two: B beats D because purge methods defeat recovery on solid-state drives, while a standard overwrite can miss cells hidden by wear leveling.
Exam cue: deleting is not sanitizing. Match the method, clear, purge or destroy, to the media type and data sensitivity, and keep a record.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 Section 3.1 (Sanitization Methods: clear, purge and destroy); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 MP-6 (Media Sanitization)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A4.2 Retention and Sanitization (deleting is not sanitizing; method matched to media). Original school district laptop donation scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D4 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): B drops the key-only 'and record it' virtue.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Investment prioritization
questions.question: A hospital's investment committee can fund one of two projects with similar returns; one would retire a system tied to a high-rated patient-safety risk. What is the MOST useful input from the risk practitioner?

options.A: The risk logs each project manager keeps for their own project
options.B: A ranking of the two projects by projected return on investment
options.C: A new rating of the patient-safety risk against the hospital's appetite
options.D: A comparison of how each project changes the enterprise risk profile

questions.key_concept: Portfolio decisions weigh value and risk together, including the enterprise risk a project would reduce.
questions.pre_read: Note what the two projects share and what separates them, then ask which information shows that difference.
questions.correct_explanation: With returns roughly equal, the deciding difference is risk. Showing how each project would change the enterprise risk profile, including the patient-safety risk one would reduce, lets the committee weigh value and risk together and make the call. Re-rating the patient-safety risk, already rated high, sizes one effect but misses any risk the other project would reduce or add, so it cannot settle the comparison.

wrong_explanations.A: Project logs track delivery risks such as delay and budget overrun, not how each choice changes the enterprise's exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Return alone cannot separate two projects with similar returns, and it hides the risk reduction one of them offers.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it sizes the risk one project would retire. But the committee is comparing two projects, so it needs each one's effect on the whole risk profile.

tips: Eliminate: B ranks on return, which cannot separate projects with similar returns, and A offers project delivery logs that do not show enterprise exposure.
Final two: D beats C because the committee is choosing between two projects; rating one risk alone misses what else each project adds or removes.
Exam cue: in portfolio items, the practitioner gives decision-makers value and risk together, including risks a project would reduce; the committee decides.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-03 (cybersecurity risk management activities and outcomes are included in enterprise risk management processes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A5.1 Portfolio Management by Value and Risk (score value and risk together, counting risks a project reduces). Original hospital investment scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D4 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): strawman C replaced with a real runner-up (re-rate the safety risk); explanations and tips reworked; options re-lettered (key now D) to break the key cycle.

questions.subtopic: 4A5 Portfolio and project management. Project risk log in Agile delivery
questions.question: A pension fund's Agile project keeps its own risk log, where the scrum team has marked as accepted a weak access control that will remain after go-live. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the scrum team to fix the access control next sprint
options.B: Record the team's acceptance in the register and monitor it later
options.C: Raise it with the business risk owner in the enterprise register
options.D: Have the business product owner hold the release until it is fixed

questions.key_concept: Project risks that outlive the project go to the enterprise register and the business risk owner for a decision.
questions.pre_read: Notice who marked the entry accepted and how long the weakness will last.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk that will outlive the project becomes an operational risk, so a scrum team cannot accept it on the enterprise's behalf. Raising it in the enterprise register with the business risk owner puts the decision with someone who can accept it within appetite or require treatment. Asking the team to fix it may be the eventual answer, but choosing the response before the owner weighs the risk skips the decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: fixing the weakness may be right. But the team would be choosing the response; the owner first decides whether to fix, compensate or accept.
wrong_explanations.B: Recording the team's acceptance treats a delivery team as the risk owner. Operational risk after go-live must be accepted by the accountable business owner.
wrong_explanations.D: A product owner runs the backlog, not the operational risk; holding the release picks a response before the business risk owner has weighed it.

tips: Eliminate: B lets a delivery team accept an operational risk, and D has the product owner hold the release, a response chosen before the business risk owner decides.
Final two: C beats A because the owner decides the response first; asking the team to fix it picks a treatment before the right person has weighed the risk.
Exam cue: project risks that remain after go-live move to the enterprise register and the business owner; delivery teams do not accept them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-03 (cybersecurity risk management activities and outcomes are included in enterprise risk management processes); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A5.2 Project Risk and Agile Delivery (exam trap: project risk log kept apart from the enterprise register). Original pension fund Agile scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D4 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Cross-domain fix 30 Oct 2026: 'business' added to distractor D so the lens word is not key-only.

questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Shared recovery dependency
questions.question: A payroll provider's disaster recovery site is in another city but relies on the same internet carrier as its main data center. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Assess whether losing the shared carrier would breach the payroll RTO
options.B: Move the recovery site to a city served by a different carrier
options.C: Recommend that the owner fund a second carrier for the recovery site
options.D: Assess the carrier's outage history and service-level commitments

questions.key_concept: A dependency shared by primary and recovery sites is analyzed against recovery objectives before a treatment is chosen.
questions.pre_read: Look for anything the two sites have in common, then weigh what each option assumes is already known.
questions.correct_explanation: A shared carrier is a single point of failure that could take down both sites, but the size of the risk depends on what an outage would do to payroll recovery. Assessing it against the recovery time objective (RTO) shows whether the exposure is within tolerance and what treatment is justified. A second carrier may well be the answer, yet recommending it before analysis skips the cost-benefit judgment the owner needs.

wrong_explanations.B: Relocating the site is a costly treatment chosen before the risk is analyzed, and the RTO might be met far more cheaply.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: diverse carriers remove the shared dependency. But the practitioner first analyzes the impact so the owner can weigh the fix against its cost.
wrong_explanations.D: Outage history and service levels describe the carrier, not the effect of losing it. A service credit does not get payroll out on time.

tips: Eliminate: D gathers assurances about the carrier rather than the impact of losing it, and B jumps to a costly relocation before the risk is sized.
Final two: A beats C because analysis comes before treatment; the RTO comparison tells the owner whether a second carrier is worth its cost.
Exam cue: when a recovery design shares a dependency with production, first measure the impact against RTO and RPO, then recommend a treatment.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CP-8(2) (Telecommunications Services | Single Points of Failure); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Section 3.2.1 (Determine Business Processes and Recovery Criticality: MTD, RTO and RPO)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A6.1 Recovery Strategies and Alternate Sites (shared dependencies are single points of failure; judge the design against RTO). questions.subtopic: 4A6 Technology resilience and disaster response/recovery. Ransomware restore sequence
questions.question: Ransomware has encrypted a distributor's order system, and the operations director urges an immediate restore from last night's backup to resume shipping. What should the risk practitioner advise as the BEST next step?

options.A: Restore the order system from last night's backup without delay
options.B: Contain the attack and verify the backup is clean before restoring
options.C: Pay the ransom if it costs less than the expected outage losses
options.D: Restore from an older backup, taken before the attack likely began

questions.key_concept: During ransomware recovery, contain the attack and verify backup integrity before restoring.
questions.pre_read: Notice the pressure in the stem and what is still unknown about the attack.
questions.correct_explanation: Restoring while the attacker still has access, or from a backup that holds the malware, invites a second encryption and a longer outage. Containing the attack and verifying the backup is clean comes first, then restoration. An older backup lowers the chance of restoring malware, but without containment the attacker can simply encrypt the restored system again, and an older copy also loses more orders.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is fastest. But if the attacker is still inside or the backup carries the malware, restored systems are encrypted again.
wrong_explanations.C: Paying is a senior management and legal decision, does not guarantee recovery and may breach sanctions rules; it is not a choice made on cost alone.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: an older copy is less likely to hold malware. But without containment the attacker can re-encrypt it, and it loses more data.

tips: Eliminate: A restores into a live attack, and C reduces a legal and senior management decision about paying criminals to a cost comparison.
Final two: B beats D because containment must come first; an older backup without containment can be encrypted again and costs extra lost data.
Exam cue: in ransomware recovery the order is contain, verify the backup is clean, then restore, even under pressure to resume quickly.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 RS.MI-01 (incidents are contained); NIST CSF 2.0 RC.RP-03 (the integrity of backups and other restoration assets is verified before using them for restoration)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A6.2 Backups and Ransomware Recovery (contain, verify the backup is clean, then restore). questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. Vendor claims for a new platform
questions.question: A retail bank's innovation team wants to adopt a blockchain trade-finance platform, citing the vendor's claim that it is tamper-proof. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Approve a limited pilot relying on the ledger's tamper-proof design
options.B: Rate the platform above appetite until the technology has matured
options.C: Assess its risks and benefits against the bank's objectives and appetite
options.D: Assess the vendor's controls through independent security certification

questions.key_concept: Emerging technology is assessed for both risks and benefits against objectives and appetite before adoption.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the vendor claims from what the bank still needs to know about its own use.
questions.correct_explanation: A vendor's tamper-proof claim covers the ledger, not the bank's whole use: key management, smart-contract errors, legal standing and integration all carry risk, and the platform may also offer real gains. Assessing risks and benefits against objectives and appetite gives senior management a basis to adopt, adapt or decline. Independent certification is useful evidence within that assessment, but it describes vendor controls, not fit.

wrong_explanations.A: Tamper evidence does not stop fraud through stolen keys or false data entered at the start, and approving is not the practitioner's call.
wrong_explanations.B: Rating it above appetite before any analysis forgoes possible value; uncertainty calls for assessment, not a reflex no.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: certification tests the vendor's claims. But it covers the vendor's controls at a point in time, not the bank's use, benefits or appetite.

tips: Eliminate: A takes the vendor's design claim as proof and has the practitioner approve, and B rates the platform above appetite without weighing its benefits or risks.
Final two: C beats D because a fit-specific assessment of risks and benefits is the basis for the decision; certification is one input about vendor controls.
Exam cue: for emerging technology, assess both threats and opportunities against objectives and appetite before anyone adopts or bans it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-07 (strategic opportunities or positive risks are characterized and are included in organizational cybersecurity risk discussions); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-10 (critical suppliers are assessed prior to acquisition)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A7.1 Evaluating Emerging Technologies (neither ban nor adopt on vendor claims; weigh threats and opportunities). Original bank blockchain scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE or prep-bank text used. CRISC D4 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): A loses its 'since' tail; 'appetite' added to B and 'assess' to D (blind de-cue); why-B and tip 1 updated; B length evened.

questions.subtopic: 4A7 Emerging technologies. High-impact AI before go-live
questions.question: A city council plans to rank housing-assistance applications with a vendor's AI tool that scored well in tests on the vendor's own data. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Accept the vendor's test results as evidence of the tool's fairness
options.B: Test the tool for bias and accuracy on past council applications
options.C: Have caseworkers review every ranking before any decision is issued
options.D: Limit the tool to ranking applications from a single district at first

questions.key_concept: High-impact AI is assessed on the organization's own data and use before controls are chosen or the tool goes live.
questions.pre_read: Notice whose data the vendor's tests used, and how serious the decisions are for the people ranked.
questions.correct_explanation: Housing-assistance rankings affect people's lives, and tests on the vendor's data say little about bias or accuracy for the council's applicants. Testing the tool on past council applications comes first, because it shows whether the risk is within appetite and which controls are needed. Caseworker review is a likely control, but adding it before the test chooses a treatment blind, and reviewers tend to follow a biased ranking.

wrong_explanations.A: Vendor tests use the vendor's data and goals. The council remains accountable for decisions about its applicants and needs results on its own population.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: human review is a strong control for high-impact AI. But it is a treatment chosen before the risk is known, and reviewers often defer to rankings.
wrong_explanations.D: A smaller rollout still exposes real applicants in that district to an unassessed tool; limiting scope does not replace assessment.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts the vendor's own tests as proof for a different population, and D narrows the rollout but still runs an unassessed tool on real applicants.
Final two: B beats C because assessment comes before treatment; human oversight will likely be part of the answer, but only local bias and accuracy results show what kind and how much.
Exam cue: for high-impact AI, the FIRST step is an assessment on the organization's own data and use, then controls such as human oversight.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MEASURE 2.11 (fairness and bias as identified in the MAP function are evaluated and results are documented); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MEASURE 2.3 (AI system performance or assurance criteria are measured and demonstrated for conditions similar to deployment settings)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4A7.2 AI and Machine Learning Adoption (assess AI use against appetite before go-live; vendor reputation does not transfer accountability). questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. Conflicting duties
questions.question: A risk practitioner finds that one employee at a charity's finance office can add new suppliers, approve their invoices and release payments. Which security principle does this MOST directly violate?

options.A: Separation of duties: one person runs the full payment cycle
options.B: Least privilege: the employee holds unusually broad finance access
options.C: Defense in depth: payments depend on a single control layer
options.D: Need to know: the employee can view every supplier record

questions.key_concept: Separation of duties splits conflicting steps of a process so no one person can complete and conceal misuse alone.
questions.pre_read: List the steps one person controls, then match the risk to the principle each option names.
questions.correct_explanation: Adding suppliers, approving invoices and releasing payments are conflicting duties: together they let one person create a fake supplier, approve its invoice and pay it, with no one else involved. That is a separation of duties failure. Least privilege is the close runner-up, but each right might be justified for some finance role; the danger comes from combining them in one person.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the access is broad. But least privilege asks whether each right is needed; the real flaw is that one person holds every conflicting step.
wrong_explanations.C: Defense in depth is about layering different controls around an asset; the core issue here is who holds which duties in one process.
wrong_explanations.D: Need to know limits who can view information. The risk here is not viewing supplier data but completing a payment fraud alone.

tips: Eliminate: C concerns layers of controls and D concerns who may view information; neither addresses one person completing a whole transaction.
Final two: A beats B because the danger is the combination of conflicting duties; least privilege judges each right alone, separation of duties judges the set.
Exam cue: when one person can initiate, approve and execute the same transaction, the principle at stake is separation of duties.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 AC-5 (Separation of Duties)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4B1.1 Core Security Principles (separation of duties versus least privilege). questions.subtopic: 4B1 Security concepts, frameworks and standards. Framework alignment and ratings
questions.question: A bank's NIST CSF 2.0 Current Profile now matches its Target Profile, so the CIO proposes lowering every cyber risk rating in the register by one level. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Treat the matched profiles as proof every scenario is now low
options.B: Lower every rating by one level across the register at once
options.C: Keep ratings until an auditor certifies the profile as evidence
options.D: Rerate each scenario on evidence before any rating changes

questions.key_concept: Framework alignment is evidence about controls; a risk rating changes only when the scenario's likelihood and impact are reassessed.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a framework profile measures and what a risk rating measures.
questions.correct_explanation: A profile shows which framework outcomes the bank achieves; it does not measure the likelihood and impact of each risk scenario. Ratings in the register change when each scenario is reassessed, using evidence such as control test results, threats and impacts. Waiting for an auditor to certify the profile still treats framework alignment as the trigger, so even a certified match would not show how any single rating should move.

wrong_explanations.A: Profiles describe outcomes achieved, not exposure. A bank can meet its Target Profile and still face scenarios rated high for impact or threat level.
wrong_explanations.B: A blanket one-level cut skips analysis; some scenarios may not depend on the improved outcomes, and others may face new threats.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it refuses the blanket cut. But certifying the profile only confirms alignment again; ratings move when each scenario is reassessed.

tips: Eliminate: A treats framework alignment as proof of low risk, and B cuts every rating at once without analyzing any scenario.
Final two: D beats C because a rating reflects a scenario's likelihood and impact; certifying the profile confirms alignment but reassesses nothing.
Exam cue: framework alignment and certification are evidence about controls; risk ratings change only when scenarios are reassessed.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 Section 3.1 (CSF Profiles: a Current Profile describes outcomes being achieved and a Target Profile the outcomes selected for risk management objectives); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-05 (threats, vulnerabilities, likelihoods and impacts are used to understand inherent risk and inform risk response prioritization)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4B1.3 Security Frameworks and Standards (frameworks organize and benchmark; risk assessment decides). questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Training matched to the role
questions.question: A parcel carrier's annual security course is the same for all staff, yet most shared-login incidents involve seasonal warehouse workers in their first month. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Discipline seasonal workers found sharing a scanner login
options.B: Lengthen the annual course and repeat it for every staff member
options.C: Add role-based login training to seasonal workers' onboarding
options.D: Lock warehouse scanners after one minute without activity

questions.key_concept: Awareness training is targeted at the roles and moments where the risk arises, not delivered as one course for everyone.
questions.pre_read: Notice who is involved in most incidents and when, then check when each option would reach them.
questions.correct_explanation: The incidents cluster in one role at one time: seasonal workers in their first month, often before the annual course even reaches them. Adding role-based login training to their onboarding puts the right content at the moment the risk arises. Lengthening the annual course adds volume for every role yet still arrives too late for workers who start and leave within one season.

wrong_explanations.A: Discipline treats a training gap as misconduct; new workers may never have been shown how scanner logins should work, so sharing would continue.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it adds training. But it adds volume for every role and still arrives after the first month, when most incidents happen.
wrong_explanations.D: A faster lockout adds sign-in friction for busy new workers, which tends to increase login sharing rather than prevent it.

tips: Eliminate: A punishes a training gap as misconduct, and D adds sign-in friction that tends to encourage the sharing it aims to stop.
Final two: C beats B because the risk sits in one role at one moment; targeted onboarding reaches it, while a longer course for everyone arrives too late.
Exam cue: when incidents cluster in one role or stage, target training at that role and moment instead of adding general awareness for all.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AT-01 (personnel are provided with awareness and training so that they possess the knowledge and skills to perform general tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-01 (organizational leadership is responsible and accountable for cybersecurity risk and fosters a culture that is risk-aware, ethical and continually improving)

questions.subtopic: 4B2 Security/risk awareness and training. Measuring awareness of AI use
questions.question: A law firm reports 98% completion of AI-use training, but its data-loss tool still flags client files uploaded to public chatbots. Which measure should the risk practitioner track to BEST show awareness is working?

options.A: The monthly trend in documents sent to unapproved AI services
options.B: The number of AI tools added to the blocked-website list
options.C: The share of staff who complete the AI-use course each year
options.D: Average staff scores on the quiz that ends the AI-use course

questions.key_concept: Awareness is measured by changes in risky behavior, not by course completion or quiz scores.
questions.pre_read: Notice the gap between the training figure and the tool's alerts, then ask what each measure would show.
questions.correct_explanation: Awareness aims to change behavior, so the best measure tracks the risky behavior itself. A falling trend in documents sent to unapproved AI services would show staff acting differently, which is what reduces the risk to client data. Quiz scores show what staff know right after the course, and completion shows who attended; completion is already high while uploads continue, which proves knowing is not doing.

wrong_explanations.B: Counting blocked tools measures a technical control's reach, not whether staff awareness or behavior has changed.
wrong_explanations.C: Completion is already 98% while uploads continue, which shows attendance does not measure safer behavior.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: quiz scores test understanding. But staff can pass a quiz and still upload files under deadline pressure; knowledge is not behavior.

tips: Eliminate: C measures attendance, which is already high while uploads continue, and B counts a technical control rather than any change in staff behavior.
Final two: A beats D because the goal of awareness is safer behavior; quiz scores show knowledge, the upload trend shows what staff actually do.
Exam cue: the BEST awareness metric tracks the risky behavior itself over time, not course completion or test scores.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 Section 5.2.3 (Evaluating CPLP Effectiveness); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.AT-01 (personnel are provided with awareness and training so that they possess the knowledge and skills to perform general tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind)

questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. New use of customer data
questions.question: A retailer collects purchase history for its loyalty program, encrypts it and restricts access, and marketing now wants to infer customers' health conditions from it for ads. What PRIMARY concern should the risk practitioner raise?

options.A: Attackers could steal the encryption keys and expose the history
options.B: Marketing staff may lack training in secure data handling
options.C: Customers may ask for copies of their purchase data
options.D: The new use exceeds the purpose the data was collected for

questions.key_concept: Privacy governs whether a use of personal data fits its stated purpose; security only protects the data from unauthorized access.
questions.pre_read: Note what the retailer already does well, then ask what the new proposal changes.
questions.correct_explanation: Purpose limitation means personal data is used only for the purposes stated when it was collected. Inferring health conditions from purchases for ads is a new and sensitive purpose customers never agreed to, whatever the encryption. Strong security keeps outsiders out but does not make an unfair use by authorized staff acceptable. Access requests are a real privacy right, but they are not what this proposal puts at risk.

wrong_explanations.A: Key theft is a security risk the encryption and access limits already address; the concern this proposal raises is how authorized staff will use the data.
wrong_explanations.B: Training affects how safely staff handle data, not whether this new use is allowed.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: access requests are a real privacy right. But the proposal's problem is a new, sensitive use that customers did not agree to.

tips: Eliminate: A and B are security and handling concerns about data that is already well protected; neither asks whether the new use is permitted.
Final two: D beats C because the proposal creates a new, sensitive use beyond the stated purpose; access rights matter but are not what this change threatens.
Exam cue: privacy asks whether a use is fair and fits the stated purpose; strong encryption never answers that question.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 PT-3 (Personally Identifiable Information Processing Purposes); NIST Privacy Framework Version 1.0 Section 1.2.1 (Cybersecurity and Privacy Risk Management: privacy risk can arise from data processing unrelated to cybersecurity incidents)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 4B3.1 Privacy Principles (privacy is not security; encryption does not make an unfair use acceptable). questions.subtopic: 4B3 Data privacy and data protection principles. Privacy impact assessment updates
questions.question: A gym chain's member app passed a privacy impact assessment at launch and will now share workout data with an insurance partner. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Confirm the launch assessment still applies to the unchanged app
options.B: Update the privacy impact assessment to cover the new insurer sharing
options.C: Collect fresh consent from members before any data is shared
options.D: Encrypt the workout data before it is sent to the insurance partner

questions.key_concept: A privacy impact assessment is updated before new processing starts when purpose, data or recipients change.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the original assessment covered and what is new about the planned sharing.
questions.correct_explanation: A privacy impact assessment (PIA) describes the processing it assessed. Sharing workout data with an insurer is a new purpose and a new recipient, so the PIA must be updated before sharing starts, to judge the risk to members and show which protections the owner needs. Fresh consent may be one of those protections, but choosing it first skips the analysis that shows whether consent is the right basis or is enough.

wrong_explanations.A: The app may be unchanged, but the processing is not: a new purpose and recipient are exactly what the launch assessment never covered.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: consent may be needed. But it is one possible measure; the updated assessment decides whether it is the right basis and what else is required.
wrong_explanations.D: Encryption protects data in transit, but it does not decide whether sharing health-related data with an insurer is fair or lawful.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an unchanged app as unchanged processing, and D offers a security control that does not decide whether the sharing is acceptable.
Final two: B beats C because the assessment comes before the mitigation; consent may be part of the answer, but the updated PIA shows what is required.
Exam cue: a privacy impact assessment is updated whenever the purpose, data or recipients change, before the new processing starts.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-8 (Privacy Impact Assessments)
